title: Research UCC Warranty Disclaimer Requirements for New Product Launch

blind.coverage: I read the instructions and all 45 criteria. I read these documents in full: the Ogilvie assignment email (including Priya Dasgupta's forwarded email), the CIT Standard Limited Warranty, the marketing brochure, the sales deck, the sales team instruction memo, the draft quotation letter, and the Stoneridge letter. I read most of the 2021 Birchwood, Sato & Klein memo (the executive summary, scope, background, sections IV–VIII, and the recommendations). I read the Summary and Pending Claims sheets of the claims spreadsheet and searched the Claim Detail sheet for specific facts. I checked the record facts behind each criterion: 12-point Times New Roman, in-box warranty delivery, the email campaign language, the $8,500 cartridges, 47/62/71 claims, $680K settlements, and the $1.2M Redmond claim. From primary sources I read Cal. Civ. Code § 1791(a)–(b) and 15 U.S.C. § 2301(1). I did not read primary texts for the Texas procurement statutes, Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 2.316, UCC §§ 1-201(b)(10), 2-313, 2-316, or 2-719, or the shrinkwrap cases. For those I relied on general knowledge and the statutory text quoted in the BSK memo. I did not run a solver or judge.

findings.title: Song-Beverly criterion requires saying an agricultural co-op buying commercial irrigation equipment 'could arguably' be a consumer-goods buyer
findings.explanation: Song-Beverly reaches only 'consumer goods', meaning goods bought 'primarily for personal, family, or household purposes', and a buyer must be an 'individual'. Harmon Valley is an entity. It is buying $475K–$525K industrial systems for irrigation and processing. Both definitional elements fail on their face. A competent memo would flag Song-Beverly (the assignment asks for it) and conclude it almost certainly does not apply. The PASS condition instead requires 'noting that agricultural cooperatives purchasing goods for use by members could arguably fall within the Act's scope as consumer goods purchasers.' A judge could fail the correct conclusion for not taking that position, and the criterion rewards a legally weak one. Its accurate point, that Song-Beverly's disclaimer limits are stricter than the UCC's, only matters if the Act applies.

evidence.quote: noting that agricultural cooperatives purchasing goods for use by members could arguably fall within the Act's scope as 'consumer goods' purchasers
focus on irrigation water quality, crop protection, and the long-term value of clean water in maximizing yield
Check whether any of the consumer warranty statutes could reach this transaction.

authorities.proposition: 'Consumer goods' means any new product bought or used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes.
'Buyer' or 'retail buyer' means any individual who buys consumer goods from a retail seller.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo flags Song-Beverly as a California consumer-warranty statute the co-op structure raises, and analyzes whether it applies (consumer goods / individual buyer), whatever the conclusion. Drop the requirement to call coverage 'arguable'.

findings.title: 'Email campaign' language comes only from the broker's description; the identical sentence is in the brochure
findings.explanation: No email campaign document is in the record, and the assignment's document list does not include one. The quoted sentence appears word for word in the marketing brochure. Only the Stoneridge letter calls it 'email campaign language.' A careful solver could correctly attribute the sentence to the brochure and analyze it as express-warranty language. It might never mention an 'email campaign', since that campaign is not in the record. A strict judge could then fail C-027, even though the memo covered the exact language. The criterion rewards sourcing from a secondhand description over the primary document.

evidence.quote: The email campaign language promises "98.5% uptime and 99.97% purity—that's our commitment to your operations."
With the AquaPure Max 9000, you can count on 98.5% uptime and 99.97% purity --- that's our commitment to your operations.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo identifies the 'you can count on 98.5% uptime and 99.97% purity—that's our commitment' language (whether attributed to the brochure or the proposed email campaign) as a source of express warranty.

findings.title: BSK memo describes a different 'March 15, 2021' warranty than the one supplied
findings.explanation: The BSK memo reviews the warranty 'revised March 15, 2021'. It quotes a shorter disclaimer and cap, and says the document has no integration clause, no governing-law or forum clause, no registration system, and no section headings setting off the disclaimer. The supplied warranty has the same revision date and document number, but it contains an entire-agreement clause (7.3), Oregon law and forum clauses (7.1–7.2), a registration section (8), an independence-of-remedy clause (6), and a bold, underlined all-caps 'SECTION 5: DISCLAIMER OF WARRANTIES' heading. That heading is a UCC § 1-201(b)(10)(A) example of a conspicuous term. This makes the record unclear on which BSK recommendations were adopted (C-041, C-011), and it undercuts C-006's premise that nothing visually sets the disclaimer apart. Ogilvie says nothing was implemented, which conflicts with the supplied document. The criteria are still passable, but a solver who notices the conflict and reports it accurately could be graded unpredictably.

evidence.quote: The current Warranty Document does not contain a clear integration clause
The current Warranty Document does not specify a governing law or a dispute resolution mechanism
This Warranty, together with CIT's standard purchase order terms and conditions, constitutes the entire agreement between CIT and Buyer
CIT never implemented those recommendations. The only change that was made was the uppercase text formatting

findings.suggested_fix: Make the BSK memo's quoted text and description match the supplied warranty, or date the supplied warranty after the memo. Relax C-006 so that a memo that notes the section heading but still flags the same-size, non-bold body text passes.

findings.title: Texas criterion offers Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 2.316 as a Texas-specific rule that 'may differ from standard UCC'
findings.explanation: Texas § 2.316 is Texas's enactment of UCC 2-316 and is uniform on everything relevant here. Citing it identifies no Texas-specific difference. The Texas-specific risks for a sale to a municipal water authority lie elsewhere: the local-government contract immunity waiver and its damages limits, procurement statutes, and possibly the DTPA, which counts governmental subdivisions as consumers. Because § 2.316 is an approved example, a memo that only cites it for Triton could pass without identifying any real Texas-specific exposure. The criterion is mostly sound but can reward a hollow answer.

evidence.quote: flags Texas-specific warranty or procurement requirements that may differ from standard UCC provisions, such as Texas Business & Commerce Code § 2.316 or Texas governmental procurement rules

authorities.proposition: Texas enactment of UCC 2-316 (disclaimer of implied warranties), substantively uniform on the points at issue

findings.suggested_fix: Remove § 2.316 as an example. Require identification of a genuinely Texas- or government-specific issue, such as governmental immunity or damages limits for local-government contracts, procurement requirements, or DTPA exposure.

findings.title: Cartridge-tying criterion lists Magnuson-Moss implications, which cannot apply to industrial equipment
findings.explanation: The MMWA anti-tying rule and its other duties apply only to 'consumer products': property 'normally used for personal, family, or household purposes.' A $475K, 8,500-lb industrial purification system is not one. The BSK memo in the record says as much. The criterion is disjunctive (antitrust tying OR MMWA), so a correct memo that relies on antitrust or UCC 2-719 unconscionability should pass. But the criterion would also reward a memo that wrongly treats the MMWA as governing the cartridge requirement.

evidence.quote: including potential tying concerns under antitrust law or Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act implications
CIT's industrial water purification systems are not, in the ordinary course, "consumer products" within the meaning of the MMWA.

authorities.proposition: 'Consumer product' means tangible personal property normally used for personal, family, or household purposes.

findings.suggested_fix: Reword to 'potential tying/antitrust concerns, or an explanation of why Magnuson-Moss does or does not apply', so that misapplying the MMWA is not rewarded.

blind.overall: Overall the rubric is sound and closely tracks the record and the assignment email. Most of the 45 criteria are items Ogilvie explicitly asked for, or standard parts of a UCC warranty memo, and they rest on accurate facts: the brochure, deck, and sales memo quotations, the 12-point Times New Roman formatting, in-box warranty delivery, the claims data, and the Redmond litigation. The statements of UCC §§ 2-313, 2-316(1)–(2), 1-201(b)(10), and 2-719(2) are accurate. The main legal defect is C-016: it requires asserting that an agricultural cooperative buying commercial irrigation equipment could arguably be a Song-Beverly consumer-goods buyer, which the statute's definitions foreclose. Smaller issues are the email-campaign attribution in C-027, a real inconsistency between the BSK memo's description of the warranty and the supplied warranty, and loose Texas and MMWA examples that could reward thin or wrong answers. Under all-pass scoring, C-016 is the criterion most likely to fail a legally correct memo.

sol_verdicts.reason: Cal. Civ. Code § 1791(a) limits 'consumer goods' to goods bought primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, and § 1791(b) limits 'buyer' to an individual. Harmon Valley is an entity buying industrial irrigation and processing systems. The PASS condition requires saying the co-op 'could arguably' be a consumer-goods purchaser, so a correct memo that concludes the Act does not apply is at risk of failing.

The XML confirms Sol's point: the disclaimer runs are Times New Roman at w:sz=22 (11 pt), matching the body text. But the BSK memo in the record says 12-point, and the judge sees pandoc text with no sizes. The fact that matters, same size as the surrounding text, is correct, so this alone rarely misgrades. The bigger problem, a bold, enlarged heading, is covered in O2.

For C-006, uppercase text plus a bold, underlined, 14-pt 'SECTION 5: DISCLAIMER OF WARRANTIES' heading can meet § 1-201(b)(10)(A). A reasoned memo that finds low risk could fail the 'flag a deficiency' requirement. C-008 only asks for specific formatting recommendations. Ogilvie invites them and BSK made them, so recommending improvements is prudent whatever the risk conclusion.

The criterion says the disclaimer is 'undermined or called into question' and FAILs only a memo that ignores the tension between the disclaimer and the sales conduct. A precise memo would say reliance alone does not defeat a conspicuous § 2-316(2) disclaimer, and that post-sale delivery and express-warranty overlap are the real problems. That memo still addresses the tension and passes. The wording is soft enough to be defensible.

15 U.S.C. § 2301(1) limits the MMWA to consumer products normally used for personal, family, or household purposes. The BSK memo says CIT's industrial systems are not consumer products. The disjunctive wording lets a correct antitrust or unconscionability memo pass, but it would also reward treating the MMWA anti-tying rule as governing.

findings.explanation: Song-Beverly covers only 'consumer goods', meaning goods bought primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, and its 'buyer' must be an individual. Harmon Valley is a cooperative entity. It is buying $475K–$525K industrial systems for irrigation and processing. Both elements fail on the record facts. Ogilvie asks whether consumer statutes 'could reach' the deal, which calls for applying these limits. A competent memo would flag the Act and conclude it very likely does not apply. The PASS condition instead requires 'noting that agricultural cooperatives ... could arguably fall within the Act's scope.' So a judge could fail the correct conclusion, and the criterion rewards a legally weak position. Under all-pass scoring, this is the criterion most likely to zero out a correct memo.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo flags Song-Beverly and analyzes whether it applies (consumer goods and individual buyer), whatever it concludes. Drop the requirement to call coverage 'arguable', and reserve the risk for any facts showing personal use.

findings.title: Conspicuousness criterion misstates the font size and ignores the bold, enlarged disclaimer heading that § 1-201(b)(10)(A) recognizes
findings.explanation: C-006 requires the memo to say the disclaimer is in 'the same 12-point Times New Roman' and is not made conspicuous by 'larger font size ... or other visual differentiation', and that this 'may be legally insufficient'. In the supplied DOCX, body and disclaimer runs are 11 pt (w:sz=22). The '12-point' figure comes from the 2021 BSK memo. The disclaimer sits directly under 'SECTION 5: DISCLAIMER OF WARRANTIES', which is bold, underlined, all caps, and 14 pt. Solver and judge can both see it in the extracted text. A capitalized heading larger than the surrounding text is the first statutory example of a conspicuous term. A careful memo could reasonably conclude the heading plus the uppercase body substantially reduces the risk, and such a memo may fail for not flagging a 'deficiency.' Most memos will follow Ogilvie's lead and flag the risk anyway, so this is arguable rather than problematic.

evidence.quote: is printed in the same 12-point Times New Roman font as the rest of the document and is not made conspicuous through bolding, contrasting color, larger font size, borders, or other visual differentiation
**[SECTION 5: DISCLAIMER OF WARRANTIES]{.underline}**
This disclaimer is printed in uppercase (all capital letters) in 12-point Times New Roman typeface.
(A) a heading in capitals equal to or greater in size than the surrounding text, or in contrasting type, font, or color

findings.suggested_fix: Drop '12-point'. PASS if the memo assesses whether the disclaimer is conspicuous under § 1-201(b)(10), accounts for the uppercase body and the section heading, and gives a reasoned risk view, including a conclusion that some risk remains because the body text is the same size and not bold.

findings.title: The BSK memo and Ogilvie describe a 'March 15, 2021' warranty that lacks provisions the supplied warranty of that date contains
findings.explanation: The BSK memo reviewed the warranty 'revised March 15, 2021'. It says that document has no integration clause, no governing-law or forum clause, and no registration system, and it recommends adding them. Ogilvie says CIT 'never implemented those recommendations.' The supplied warranty has the same revision date, yet it includes an Entire Agreement clause (7.3), Oregon law and Multnomah County forum clauses (7.1–7.2), a registration section (8), and a remedy-independence clause. C-041 requires 'noting which recommendations were or were not implemented.' The record gives inconsistent answers to that question, so a solver who reports what the supplied document actually shows could be graded unpredictably. The criterion is still passable by simply referencing the memo, so the impact is limited.

evidence.quote: The current Warranty Document does not contain a clear integration clause

findings.suggested_fix: Make the supplied warranty match the BSK memo's description, or give it a later revision date. PASS any accurate account of which recommendations are reflected in the current document.

final.changes_from_blind: Split blind O3 into two findings. O2 is now a C-006-specific source conflict. It adopts Sol's font-size point, which I confirmed in the DOCX XML: disclaimer and body are w:sz=22, i.e. 11 pt, not the 12 pt the rubric and the BSK memo state. It adds the bold, underlined, 14-pt Section 5 heading as a § 1-201(b)(10)(A) conspicuous heading that the criterion ignores. O3 now covers only C-041. I dropped C-011 and C-018 from it: the pre-sale disclosure recommendation really was not implemented, and C-018 is unaffected. I rejected Sol's C-014 point and Sol's C-008 half of arguable/0 as not defects. Blind O1, O2, O4 and O5 are kept and renumbered as O1, O4, O5 and O6.
final.overall: The rubric is generally sound and follows Ogilvie's assignment and the record closely. The express-warranty, 2-316, 2-719, pre-sale disclosure, claims-data and Redmond criteria rest on accurate facts. The one clear legal defect is C-016. It requires saying an agricultural cooperative buying industrial irrigation systems could arguably be a Song-Beverly consumer-goods buyer, which § 1791(a)–(b) forecloses, so it can fail a correct memo. C-006 is arguable. It states the wrong point size (11 pt in the DOCX, 12 pt per the BSK memo) and ignores a bold, enlarged disclaimer heading that bears directly on conspicuousness. The remaining issues are lower-impact: a record inconsistency about which BSK recommendations were implemented (C-041), the email-campaign attribution (C-027), and loose Texas and MMWA examples that could reward thin or wrong answers (C-015, C-021).
final.coverage: I read all 45 criteria, the instructions, and Sol's index entry and report. In the first pass I read the key documents in full or nearly in full, and in this pass I re-checked the passages that bear on the findings. I inspected the warranty DOCX XML directly: 95 runs at w:sz=22, the Section 5 heading at w:sz=28 bold and underlined, and the disclaimer runs at 22 and not bold. I also grepped for 'email campaign' and for the 12-point facts, and compared the BSK memo's description of the warranty with the supplied warranty's sections 7.1–7.3 and 8. I verified Cal. Civ. Code § 1791(a)–(b) and 15 U.S.C. § 2301(1) in the first pass. I did not read the primary texts of the Texas statutes or of UCC 1-201 and 2-316. I ran no solver or judge.
